newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Swedish PM Persson faces icy wind of voter ire.
newsitem.headline: Swedish PM Persson faces icy wind of voter ire.

text.p: Swedish Prime Minister Goran Persson, accused of an arrogant hunger for power, is feeling an icy wind of discontent from voters which may scupper prospects of Sweden joining European Monetary Union, analysts say.
As deep winter spreads over Sweden, Persson spent the Christmas holiday mulling opinion polls that show his minority government would be demolished if elections were held soon.
Opponents have accused Persson of masking a concentration of power with legal changes which took effect from January 1 that changed the administrative status of government departments.
"This is typical Persson; all power to the prime minister. Ministers have become nothing more than departmental heads in cabinet," said former defence minister Anders Bjorck.
Since taking over from mild-mannered Ingvar Carlsson a year ago, Persson has seen support for his minority Social Democratic government plunge to 30 percent, its lowest since 1991.

Liberal daily Dagens Nyheter, which generally supports the government, said Persson's position would be in severe doubt if such figures were reflected in general elections, not due until September 1998.

While Persson's position appears safe until then, he has come under unprecedented attack from Swedes this winter and may be forced to drop his previously-stated support for Swedish membership of the EU's Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) and EMU.
Sweden only joined the EU a year ago, but Euro-scepticism is running higher than ever and a recent poll showed 44 percent of Swedes opposed to EMU and less than one-third in favour.

Persson has said a recommendation will be made this spring by the Social Democratic Party's all-important leadership for agreement by a full party congress in September. In the meantime, he has called for broad public debate on membership.
In a newspaper article, Persson distanced himself from his previous support for EMU, possibly sensing the political folly of supporting Europe's monetary union.
"The EU would be transformed into something completely different than the EU the Swedish people, after some pain and a long and trying debate, approved," he said.
This winter the chunky Persson, who used to shrug off criticism with a jovial smile and a cutting retort, has retreated into his shell in the face of vocal insults.
He was booed by party supporters when he laid responsiblity for economic problems at the feet of the former government.

Persson has continued the conservative economic policies of former Prime Minister Carl Bildt, launching an even more ambitious programme of spending cuts that has been deeply unpopular with Swedes but which won plaudits from economists.
"Goran Persson personifies the sort of society that instils fear," said Birger Schlaug, head of the left-wing Greens Party.
Persson also scored a clumsy own goal by praising China during an official visit. He survived a rare vote of confidence in parliament over the gaffe.
Persson has had the Swedish political arena to himself since taking office. His most potent rival, Bildt, has been international mediator in Bosnia since losing the 1994 election.

But Bildt, a respected and articulate opponent who passionately supports European integration, is set to return to the domestic political fray this year and could make Persson's life even more difficult. REUTER
